titulo: The green cross before the hospital
subtitulo: The Spanish pharmacy triages you, treats you and sends you home — and when it is the wallet rather than the stomach, the counter at the comisaría has five sentences of its own
permissao: In a real emergency you dial 112 and you speak English. That is exactly what the number is for, nobody is marking your accent, and the operator is not the person you need Spanish for — the person standing next to you on the pavement is.
espelho: Standing quietly inside the door of a waiting room until somebody notices you is the bit that reads as odd there. Everybody sitting down said one sentence out loud when they arrived, and the person who says nothing is read as waiting for a friend, not as waiting for a doctor.
frasePiso: You will walk into a pharmacy, say which part of you has let you down, ask whether the box needs a prescription and come out with the right one. Most people who spend a fortnight here point at their own stomach and hope.

clique.desconto: Five sentences, and nobody handed you one of them. Three frames you already owned did the whole of it — the one that asks somebody to do something, the one that asks whether a thing exists nearby, and the one that says what you are — and not one of the three was new today.
clique.piso: You will get yourself treated in Spain with the phone in your pocket. Most people who spend a fortnight here never open their mouth at that counter.

fichasCulturais.sinal: The green cross is flashing over a shop on the corner, three people are waiting at the counter, and not one of them is holding a piece of paper from a doctor.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: This is a chemist. Plasters and sun cream, fine — but for anything that actually hurts I need a doctor, and an appointment I have not got.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The counter is the first stop in the system rather than a shop bolted onto it. The person in the white coat triages: sunburn, sore throat, a stomach in revolt, bites, a rash — and says which of them needs a doctor instead.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Say which part of you has let you down and let the counter choose the box: '¿Me puede recomendar algo para…' plus the thing that hurts.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: Four minutes at a counter gets you the thing that works, picked by somebody who does this all day, and you keep the rest of the afternoon.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not for antibiotics, and not for the strong doses of the painkillers you buy freely at home — those need a prescription here, with no exceptions, and the counter will send you to a doctor rather than bend.

fichasCulturais.sinal: Half eleven at night, the shutter is down, and there is a printed sheet taped to the inside of the glass.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: Shut is shut. I will look for a twenty-four-hour place on my phone, or wait until the morning and hope it keeps.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The area runs a rota, and that sheet is the rota. One pharmacy near you is open all night, every night, and the shut door is where the address of tonight's one is published.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Do not walk away — read the door first. And if you would rather ask a person than read a list in the dark: '¿Hay una farmacia de guardia por aquí?'
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: A night that was heading for a taxi and a waiting room turns into a five-minute walk with an address in your hand.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not instead of 112. A duty pharmacy dispenses, it does not treat — chest pain, a bad fall or a child with a fever is the phone call, not the walk.

fichasCulturais.sinal: Eleven people in a health centre waiting room in no order at all: no line on the floor, no ticket machine, nobody standing, and nobody looking at the door.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: There is no queue here. Either it is a free-for-all and I have to watch the door, or somebody is going to call my name.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The queue exists and it is held in everybody's head. It is joined out loud, once, on arrival: you ask the room who is last, one person answers, and from then on you go after that person.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Say it to the room as you come in — '¿Quién es el último?' — and remember the face that answers. When the next person asks, your answer is 'yo'.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You are in the queue from the second you arrive, and you can sit down, or step out to another counter, without losing your place.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not where there is a ticket machine or a numbered screen — a big pharmacy chain, a bank, a town hall — and asking there marks you out more than saying nothing would.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Spain sells a great deal over the counter — paracetamol and ibuprofen in standard doses, anti-inflammatories, antihistamines, decongestants, stomach remedies, creams and dressings. Antibiotics need a prescription, with no exceptions, and so do the stronger doses of the painkillers sold freely at home. Anything sold without one carries the words 'sin receta médica' on the box.
fatosDatados.fonte: docs/pesquisa-espanha.md §8.5 — marco regulatório espanhol de dispensação (2026); ibuprofeno 600 mg sempre com receita e paracetamol 1 g salvo em formatos de 10 unidades ou menos. A pesquisa marca R9: confirmar ficha AEMPS antes de regravar.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: In every locality at least one pharmacy is on duty outside shop hours, and the rota is posted on the door of every pharmacy, including the shut one you are standing in front of.
fatosDatados.fonte: docs/pesquisa-espanha.md §7.1 — rede de Colegios Oficiales de Farmacéuticos, prática nacional; fonte oficial em Madri: COFM (cofm.es → Farmacias de guardia); agregador nacional farmacias365.com

fatosDatados.afirmacao: 112 is the single emergency number in Spain — police, fire and ambulance — and it answers in English.
fatosDatados.fonte: docs/pesquisa-espanha.md §7.5 e §8.5 — UK FCDO: número único, inclui crime, atendimento em inglês disponível

fatosDatados.afirmacao: The UK GHIC gives access to medically necessary state healthcare in Spain on the same terms a resident gets, and to nothing else: it does not pay for a private clinic and it does not bring you home. GHIC gets you treated, insurance gets you home.
fatosDatados.fonte: docs/pesquisa-espanha.md §8.5 — UK GHIC válido na Espanha em centro de salud e hospital estatal, inclusive urgência e doença súbita, independentemente de condição pré-existente; não cobre repatriação, hospital privado nem nada não-médico, e o próprio governo britânico diz que não substitui seguro de viagem. Para o americano não há acordo recíproco EUA–Espanha.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: On the Costa del Sol the clinic with the English sign over the door and the English-speaking receptionist is usually a private one — which is exactly where the GHIC is worth nothing.
fatosDatados.fonte: docs/pesquisa-espanha.md §8.5 — rotulado ali como INFERÊNCIA a partir do desenho do sistema (zona britânica densa em clínicas privadas com sinalização em inglês), sem levantamento primário citado. Vai ao ar como se fosse fato e por isso está declarado aqui.

steps.pt: Part 8A. Here's the good news buried inside a bad day: in Spain, the first place you go when something's wrong with your body is not the hospital. It's the shop with the flashing green cross. The pharmacist behind that counter is trained to triage — sunburn, sore throat, a stomach in revolt, bites, a rash — and asking costs you nothing and takes four minutes, not four hours in A and E. Warm-up first, as always. Metronome hand, one tap per syllable, all the same size: far-ma-cia. Three taps, three equal taps. Flat palm: hold the vowel and don't let it slide. Five vowels. Say it, don't slide it.

Your master sentence for this entire part is a request for a recommendation: '¿Me puede recomendar algo para…?' — can you recommend me something for. Then you bolt on whichever bit of you has let you down. And note the 'puede' rather than 'puedes': a white coat behind a counter is one of the three places where 'usted' is genuinely at home. Listen.

steps.es: ¿Me puede recomendar algo para el dolor de cabeza?
steps.pinyin: meh PWEH-dheh rreh-koh-men-DAR AL-goh PAH-rah el doh-LOR deh kah-BEH-thah
steps.pt: Can you recommend me something for a headache?
steps.tts: ¿Me puede recomendar algo para el dolor de cabeza?

steps.promptPt: Four hours of sun, two hours of sleep, and your head is splitting. You're at the pharmacy counter and the pharmacist is waiting. Ask for something for a headache. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Me puede recomendar algo para el dolor de cabeza?
steps.pinyin: meh PWEH-dheh rreh-koh-men-DAR AL-goh PAH-rah el doh-LOR deh kah-BEH-thah
steps.pt: something for a headache

steps.es: ¿Es para usted? ¿Toma alguna otra medicación?
steps.pinyin: es PAH-rah oos-TEDH. TOH-mah al-GOO-nah OH-trah meh-dhee-kah-THYON
steps.pt: 👂 'Is it for you? Are you on any other medication?' — the pharmacist is triaging, not prying. Answer both.
steps.tts: ¿Es para usted? ¿Toma alguna otra medicación?

steps.promptPt: Different day, different problem: last night's calamares are staging a protest. Same sentence, swap the middle — ask for something for your stomach. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Me puede recomendar algo para el dolor de estómago?
steps.pinyin: meh PWEH-dheh rreh-koh-men-DAR AL-goh PAH-rah el doh-LOR deh ehs-TOH-mah-goh
steps.pt: something for a stomach ache
steps.tts: ¿Me puede recomendar algo para el dolor de estómago?

steps.pt: Three more endings cover most of a Spanish summer, and I'd put money on you needing at least one. 'El dolor de garganta' — sore throat. 'La diarrea' — you can work that one out on your own. 'Las quemaduras del sol' — sunburn. And 'las picaduras' — bites and stings. Same sentence every time, new ending. There's a shorter version too, if you're in a hurry and slightly desperate: '¿Tiene algo para las picaduras?' — have you got anything for bites. Both are perfectly normal. Now you.

steps.promptPt: Day two on the beach, and your partner's shoulders have gone the colour of a postbox. Ask the pharmacist for something for sunburn. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Me puede recomendar algo para las quemaduras del sol?
steps.pinyin: meh PWEH-dheh rreh-koh-men-DAR AL-goh PAH-rah lahs keh-mah-DOO-rahs del sol
steps.pt: something for sunburn
steps.tts: ¿Me puede recomendar algo para las quemaduras del sol?

steps.pt: Now the question that saves you a wasted trip. Spain sells a great deal over the counter — paracetamol, ibuprofen, antihistamines, stomach remedies, creams, sun cream, dressings. But antibiotics need a prescription, always, no exceptions, and the stronger doses of the painkillers you take at home need one too. So instead of guessing, you ask: '¿Esto necesita receta?' — does this need a prescription? And on the box itself, look for the words 'sin receta médica'. That's your green light. Listen to the question, and mind the middle of 'receta' — that's the 'th' of 'think'.

steps.es: ¿Esto necesita receta?
steps.pinyin: EHS-toh neh-theh-SEE-tah rreh-THEH-tah
steps.pt: Does this need a prescription?
steps.tts: ¿Esto necesita receta?

steps.promptPt: You've spotted the box you want on the shelf behind the counter. Before you get your hopes up, ask whether it needs a prescription. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Esto necesita receta?
steps.pinyin: EHS-toh neh-theh-SEE-tah rreh-THEH-tah
steps.pt: Does this need a prescription?

steps.es: Este no. El de seiscientos sí.
steps.pinyin: EHS-teh noh. el deh says-THYEN-tohs see
steps.pt: 👂 'This one doesn't. The six-hundred does.' — ibuprofen 600 is prescription-only here. The 400 is not.
steps.tts: Este no. El de seiscientos sí.

steps.pt: Your allergy sentence from episode four now comes back to work, except here it's about medicine rather than dinner: 'Soy alérgico a la penicilina' — or 'alérgica', if that's your ending. This is the one corner of Spanish where the -o and the -a genuinely matter, because the word is describing you. Everywhere else, relax: say 'la problema' and the pills still arrive. Here, get it right. Listen to Carmen, then give me your own version.

steps.es: Soy alérgica a la penicilina.
steps.pinyin: soy ah-LEHR-khee-kah ah lah peh-nee-thee-LEE-nah
steps.pt: I'm allergic to penicillin. (a woman speaking — note the -a)
steps.tts: Soy alérgica a la penicilina.

steps.promptPt: The pharmacist reaches for a box and you remember what's written on your medical bracelet. Tell her you're allergic to penicillin — with the ending that belongs to you. Speak now.
steps.es: Soy alérgico a la penicilina.
steps.pinyin: soy ah-LEHR-khee-koh ah lah peh-nee-thee-LEE-nah
steps.pt: I'm allergic to penicillin. (a man speaking — note the -o)
steps.tts: Soy alérgico a la penicilina.

steps.pt: GUIRI ALERT. This one is worth the price of the course on its own, and it goes off in a pharmacy. If you walk in, pat your stomach and announce 'estoy constipado', you have not told anyone you're constipated. You've told them you've got a cold. So the pharmacist hands you something for your nose, you go back to the hotel, and your actual problem carries on entirely unbothered. 'Constipado' is the head cold. Blocked in the other direction is 'estreñido'. Rule of thumb, and say it out loud once so it sticks: constipado is the nose, estreñido is everything else.

steps.es: Estoy constipado.
steps.pinyin: ehs-TOY kohns-tee-PAH-dhoh
steps.pt: 👂 'I've got a cold' — NOT 'I'm constipated'
steps.tts: Estoy constipado.

steps.pt: Now the one that turns half past eleven at night from a panic into a five-minute walk. Spain doesn't do a twenty-four-hour chemist on every corner. It does a rota: one pharmacy in the area is on duty all night, every night, and it's called 'la farmacia de guardia'. Here's the part nobody tells you, and it's pure action rather than language — when you find a pharmacy shut at night, do not walk away. Read the door. The list of tonight's duty pharmacy is printed and stuck to the glass of the closed one. And if you'd rather ask a human, this is the sentence.

steps.es: ¿Hay una farmacia de guardia por aquí?
steps.pinyin: ai OO-nah far-MAH-thyah deh GWAR-dhyah por ah-KEE
steps.pt: Is there a duty pharmacy near here?
steps.tts: ¿Hay una farmacia de guardia por aquí?

steps.promptPt: It's half eleven at night, the shutter is down, and you need something now. Stop the man walking his dog and ask whether there's a duty pharmacy nearby. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Hay una farmacia de guardia por aquí?
steps.pinyin: ai OO-nah far-MAH-thyah deh GWAR-dhyah por ah-KEE
steps.pt: Is there a duty pharmacy near here?

If the pharmacy can't fix it, two statements and one question do the rest. 'Me encuentro mal' — I feel ill. 'Me duele aquí' — it hurts here — said while pointing, which does more work than any vocabulary list you'll ever memorise. And then the question that can save you a thousand euros: '¿Esto es público o privado?' It matters most exactly where it looks least necessary — the Costa del Sol, where the clinic with the English sign and the English receptionist is usually private. If you're British, your GHIC works in the state system and nowhere else. And whoever you are, remember the line: GHIC gets you treated, insurance gets you home. Two different products, and you want both.

steps.es: Me encuentro mal. Me duele aquí.
steps.pinyin: meh en-KWEN-troh mahl · meh DWEH-leh ah-KEE
steps.pt: I feel ill. It hurts here. (and point — the finger is half the sentence)
steps.tts: Me encuentro mal. Me duele aquí.

steps.promptPt: You're at a shiny clinic in Málaga with an English sign over the door, and something about it feels a bit too smooth. Ask whether this is public or private. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Esto es público o privado?
steps.pinyin: EHS-toh es POO-blee-koh oh pree-BAH-dhoh
steps.pt: Is this public or private?
steps.tts: ¿Esto es público o privado?

steps.es: ¿Me puede dar la factura para el seguro?
steps.pinyin: meh PWEH-dheh dar lah fak-TOO-rah PAH-rah el seh-GOO-roh
steps.pt: Can I have the itemised invoice for my insurance? (no factura, no reimbursement)
steps.tts: ¿Me puede dar la factura para el seguro?

steps.pt: Two last things, and the first decides whether you get seen at all. Walk into a Spanish health centre, a market, a bakery, a fishmonger — and there is no line on the floor and nobody is standing in any order whatsoever. There is a queue. It's invisible, and you join it out loud, by asking the room: '¿Quién es el último?' — who's last? Somebody raises a hand or a chin, you go after that person, and now you exist. Don't ask, and you can stand there politely for forty minutes while the entire waiting room goes ahead of you, all of them convinced you're waiting for someone.

steps.promptPt: You push open the door of the health centre and eleven people are sitting in no discernible order. Ask, out loud, who's last. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Quién es el último?
steps.pinyin: kyen es el OOL-tee-moh
steps.pt: Who's last (in the queue)?
steps.tts: ¿Quién es el último?

steps.es: Yo. Detrás de mí ya no hay nadie.
steps.pinyin: yoh. deh-TRAHS deh MEE yah noh ai NAH-dhyeh
steps.pt: 👂 'Me. There's nobody after me.' — you are now last, and the next person through the door will ask you.
steps.tts: Yo. Detrás de mí ya no hay nadie.

steps.pt: And the real emergency. One number: 112. Police, fire, ambulance, all of it, and English is available — so here is your permission, in writing: in a genuine emergency, dial 112 and speak English. That is exactly what it's for, and nobody is marking your accent. The Spanish you need in an emergency isn't for the operator, it's for the person standing next to you on the pavement. One more thing for summer: in July and August, in the south and the interior, extreme heat is a medical matter, not a weather forecast. Two in the afternoon in Seville in August is not walking time, whatever the map says.

steps.es: Necesito una ambulancia. Es una emergencia.
steps.pinyin: neh-theh-SEE-toh OO-nah am-boo-LAN-thyah · es OO-nah eh-mehr-KHEN-thyah
steps.pt: I need an ambulance. It's an emergency. (say it to a passer-by; say 112 in English)
steps.tts: Necesito una ambulancia. Es una emergencia.

steps.es: FARMACIA DE GUARDIA · URGENCIAS · SIN RECETA MÉDICA · OLA DE CALOR
steps.pinyin: far-MAH-thyah deh GWAR-dhyah · oor-KHEN-thyahs · seen rreh-THEH-tah MEH-dhee-kah · OH-lah deh kah-LOR
steps.pt: 👂 signs: duty pharmacy · A and E / emergency department · sold without prescription · heatwave
steps.tts: Farmacia de guardia. Urgencias. Sin receta médica. Ola de calor.

steps.pt: One more thing goes wrong here, and it is the one everybody fears. Two words come first, and they are shouted.

steps.es: ¡Socorro! ¡Al ladrón!
steps.pinyin: soh-KOH-rroh · al lah-DROHN
steps.pt: Help! Stop, thief!
steps.tts: ¡Socorro! ¡Al ladrón!

steps.pt: Volume is the whole of it. A quiet English 'excuse me' has never stopped anybody, in any country, ever.

steps.promptPt: Someone has just lifted a bag off the chair next to yours and is walking away fast. Call the police — tell the people around you to call them. Speak now, and mean it.
steps.es: ¡Llame a la policía!
steps.pinyin: YAH-meh ah lah poh-lee-THEE-ah
steps.pt: Call the police!
steps.tts: ¡Llame a la policía!

steps.pt: Then the counter, and the sentence that opens it. Me han robado, and then whatever it is that has gone.

steps.es: Me han robado la cartera.
steps.pinyin: meh ahn rroh-BAH-dhoh lah kar-TEH-rah
steps.pt: My wallet's been stolen.
steps.tts: Me han robado la cartera.

steps.promptPt: You've reached for your back pocket on the way out of the metro and there is nothing there. You're at the police station counter. Tell the officer your wallet's been stolen. Speak now.
steps.es: Me han robado la cartera.
steps.pinyin: meh ahn rroh-BAH-dhoh lah kar-TEH-rah
steps.pt: My wallet's been stolen.

steps.es: ¿La ha notado en el momento o después?
steps.pinyin: lah ah noh-TAH-dhoh en el moh-MEN-toh oh dehs-PWEHS
steps.pt: 👂 'Did you feel it happen, or notice afterwards?' — they are separating a pickpocket from a robbery, and it changes the paperwork.
steps.tts: ¿La ha notado en el momento o después?

steps.pt: She wants two things and only two: where, and when. Have both ready before you reach the counter.

steps.promptPt: The officer looks up and asks where, and when. You came up off the underground about ten minutes ago. Tell her. Speak now.
steps.es: Ha sido en el metro, hace diez minutos.
steps.pinyin: ah SEE-dhoh en el MEH-troh · AH-theh dyeth mee-NOO-tohs
steps.pt: It happened on the metro, ten minutes ago.
steps.tts: Ha sido en el metro, hace diez minutos.

steps.pt: Now the sentence that decides whether any of this costs you money. No denuncia, no insurance claim. None.

steps.es: Quiero poner una denuncia.
steps.pinyin: KYEH-roh poh-NEHR OO-nah deh-NOON-thyah
steps.pt: I want to file a police report.
steps.tts: Quiero poner una denuncia.

steps.promptPt: You've explained what's gone and where. Now ask for the thing your insurer will demand: say you want to file a report. Speak now.
steps.es: Quiero poner una denuncia.
steps.pinyin: KYEH-roh poh-NEHR OO-nah deh-NOON-thyah
steps.pt: I want to file a police report.

steps.es: ¿Lleva algún documento? Sin documento no puedo tramitarla.
steps.pinyin: YEH-bah al-GOON doh-koo-MEN-toh. seen doh-koo-MEN-toh noh PWEH-dhoh trah-mee-TAR-lah
steps.pt: 👂 'Have you any ID on you? Without a document I can't process it.' — which is why the passport photo lives on your phone.
steps.tts: ¿Lleva algún documento? Sin documento no puedo tramitarla.

steps.pt: You can start it online, in English, from the hotel. But the one you filed online is only half a denuncia.
It goes live when you sign it in person at a station, and that clock is short. Same day, if you can.

steps.es: Hice la denuncia por internet. Vengo a ratificarla.
steps.pinyin: EE-theh lah deh-NOON-thyah por een-tehr-NET · BEN-goh ah rrah-tee-fee-KAR-lah
steps.pt: I filed the report online. I've come to ratify it.
steps.tts: Hice la denuncia por internet. Vengo a ratificarla.

steps.promptPt: You filed online last night and you've got the reference number on your phone. You walk into the comisaría. Tell them what you're there for. Speak now.
steps.es: Hice la denuncia por internet. Vengo a ratificarla.
steps.pinyin: EE-theh lah deh-NOON-thyah por een-tehr-NET · BEN-goh ah rrah-tee-fee-KAR-lah
steps.pt: I filed online. I've come to ratify it.
One more before you leave that counter. Your insurer wants paper, and nobody will offer it to you.

steps.es: Necesito una copia para el seguro.
steps.pinyin: neh-theh-SEE-toh OO-nah KOH-pyah PAH-rah el seh-GOO-roh
steps.pt: I need a copy for my insurance. (say it before you leave the counter)
steps.tts: Necesito una copia para el seguro.

steps.pt: Two more at that station. The first is the frame you have owned since part eight, pointed at a person.

steps.es: ¿Hay alguien que hable inglés?
steps.pinyin: ai AL-gyen keh AH-bleh een-GLEHS
steps.pt: Is there anyone who speaks English?
steps.tts: ¿Hay alguien que hable inglés?

steps.promptPt: The queue is long, your Spanish ran out two sentences ago, and there are six officers behind that desk. Ask whether one of them can do this in your own language. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Hay alguien que hable inglés?
steps.pinyin: ai AL-gyen keh AH-bleh een-GLEHS
steps.pt: Is there anyone who speaks English?

steps.es: Ahora mismo no. Puede pedir el SATE, que es para turistas.
steps.pinyin: ah-OH-rah MEES-moh noh. PWEH-dheh peh-DEER el SAH-teh, keh es PAH-rah too-REES-tahs
steps.pt: 👂 'Not right now. You can ask for the SATE — it's the tourist service.' — in the big tourist cities it exists. Ask for it by name.
steps.tts: Ahora mismo no. Puede pedir el sate, que es para turistas.

steps.pt: In the big tourist cities there is a desk built for exactly this, with interpreters. Ask for SATE by name.
And if it is the passport, the order matters. Report first, consulate second — they will ask you for it.

steps.promptPt: The worst version: the passport is gone and your flight is on Thursday. You've done the denuncia. Now say you've lost your passport and ask where the consulate is. Speak now.
steps.es: He perdido el pasaporte. ¿Dónde está el consulado?
steps.pinyin: eh pehr-DEE-dhoh el pah-sah-POR-teh · DOHN-deh ehs-TAH el kon-soo-LAH-dhoh
steps.pt: I've lost my passport. Where's the consulate?
steps.tts: He perdido el pasaporte. ¿Dónde está el consulado?

steps.pt: Back onto the street, because most of this never reaches a counter. You already own 'no, gracias' from night one.

steps.es: Déjeme en paz.
steps.pinyin: DEH-kheh-meh en pahth
steps.pt: Leave me alone. (the armoured version — flat, not shouted)
steps.tts: Déjeme en paz.

steps.pt: Flat, not shouted, and your feet never stop. Arguing is playing the game, and the game is not yours.

steps.promptPt: You said no thanks and she is still walking beside you, hand out, getting louder. Don't argue, don't explain, don't stop. One flat sentence. Speak now.
steps.es: Déjeme en paz.
steps.pinyin: DEH-kheh-meh en pahth
steps.pt: Leave me alone.
Two men in plain clothes, a badge shown too fast, and a look at your wallet. Real officers ask for ID.
The wallet stays in your pocket. One sentence ends it: a real officer shrugs and walks you there.

steps.es: Enséñeme su placa. Vamos a la comisaría.
steps.pinyin: en-SEH-nyeh-meh soo PLAH-kah · BAH-mohs ah lah koh-mee-sah-REE-ah
steps.pt: Show me your badge. Let's go to the police station.
steps.tts: Enséñeme su placa. Vamos a la comisaría.

steps.promptPt: A man in a leather jacket flashes something at you and asks, in English, to check the notes in your wallet. Keep the wallet in your pocket and give him the sentence. Speak now.
steps.es: Enséñeme su placa. Vamos a la comisaría.
steps.pinyin: en-SEH-nyeh-meh soo PLAH-kah · BAH-mohs ah lah koh-mee-sah-REE-ah
steps.pt: Show me your badge. Let's go to the police station.
And when the gift you never accepted turns up as a line on the bill, there is a sentence for that as well.

steps.es: No he pedido esto y no lo voy a pagar.
steps.pinyin: noh eh peh-DEE-dhoh EHS-toh ee noh loh boy ah pah-GAR
steps.pt: I didn't order this and I'm not paying for it. (the 'gift' that turns up on the bill)
steps.tts: No he pedido esto y no lo voy a pagar.

steps.pt: Shadowing. Say it with them, out loud, over the top — don't wait for a gap. Two sentences, and the second one is the one you'll want at midnight.

steps.es: Me encuentro mal. Me duele aquí.
steps.pinyin: meh en-KWEN-troh mahl · meh DWEH-leh ah-KEE
steps.pt: I feel ill. It hurts here.

steps.es: ¿Hay una farmacia de guardia por aquí?
steps.pinyin: ai OO-nah far-MAH-thyah deh GWAR-dhyah por ah-KEE
steps.pt: Is there a duty pharmacy near here?

The pharmacy in focus, ninety seconds. One, the template: '¿Me puede recomendar algo para…' plus the thing that hurts — 'el dolor de cabeza', 'el dolor de garganta', 'la diarrea', 'las quemaduras del sol', 'las picaduras'. Learn each one with its little article stuck to the front and stop thinking about gender entirely; the only place it matters is 'alérgico' or 'alérgica', because that word is about you. Two, 'me duele' literally means 'it hurts me' — Spanish puts the pain in charge, not you — so 'me duele aquí' plus a finger beats any word you don't know. Three, pronunciation, one last time: 'farmacia' is three beats, not four, and 'receta' has the 'th' of 'think' sitting in the middle of it. Get those two right and the pharmacist stops speaking to you slowly.

Part 8A done. The green cross triages you before the hospital ever gets involved, the door of the closed pharmacy tells you where the open one is, 112 answers in English, and '¿quién es el último?' buys you a place in a queue you can't see. In 8B — the very last part of the course — the thing everyone fears and almost nobody handles properly: 'me han robado', the police report your insurer actually requires, and a final walk past every sign in Spain that has been quietly lying to you. See you there.

steps.es: ¿Hay una farmacia de guardia por aquí?
steps.pinyin: ai OO-nah far-MAH-thyah deh GWAR-dhyah por ah-KEE
steps.pt: 'de guardia' — the word that solves the night.

aprofundar.titulo: The pharmacy, the queue and the bill (optional)

secoes.titulo: What you can buy without a prescription — and what you can't
secoes.corpo: Over the counter in Spain: paracetamol and ibuprofen in standard doses, anti-inflammatories, antihistamines, decongestants, antacids and stomach protectors, anti-diarrhoeals, creams, dressings, sun cream. Prescription only: antibiotics, with no exceptions — a pharmacy or website offering antibiotics without a prescription is breaking the law — and the higher-strength painkillers you may be used to buying freely at home. The packet of anything sold freely carries the words 'sin receta médica'. If you take something regularly, bring it with you rather than assuming you can replace it at the counter, and bring the box so the pharmacist can read the active ingredient.

exemplos.es: ¿Me puede recomendar algo para el dolor de garganta?

secoes.titulo: GHIC treats you. Insurance brings you home.
secoes.corpo: For British travellers, the UK GHIC gives access to medically necessary state healthcare in Spain on the same terms as a Spanish resident — often free or very cheap — and it covers emergencies and sudden illness regardless of pre-existing conditions. It does not cover repatriation, private hospital treatment, or anything non-medical. The UK government itself says the card is not a substitute for travel insurance. For American travellers there is no reciprocal healthcare agreement with Spain at all, US health plans typically don't pay for treatment there, and many hospitals ask non-residents to pay up front — which makes travel insurance a prerequisite rather than a nice idea. Either way, the question that protects you is the same: '¿Esto es público o privado?', asked before treatment, not after. And ask for 'la factura' — an itemised invoice — or your insurer has nothing to reimburse.

exemplos.es: ¿Me puede dar la factura para el seguro?
exemplos.pt: Can I have the invoice for my insurance?

secoes.corpo: In markets, bakeries, fishmongers, butchers, ticket windows and health centre waiting rooms, Spaniards don't form a line — they form a memory. You arrive, you ask the room '¿quién es el último?', one person acknowledges, and from then on you go after that person and the next arrival goes after you. It's efficient, it lets people wander off to another counter, and it is completely invisible to anyone who doesn't ask. If someone asks you the question later, just say 'yo' — me.

exemplos.pt: Me. / I'm last. — the answer when someone asks you

secoes.titulo: Heat is a medical item, not a weather item
secoes.corpo: Spanish summers have been breaking records, with national heat alerts and hundreds of excess deaths in a single hot month. For a visitor from a country where thirty degrees is front-page news, this changes behaviour rather than clothing: the two-to-six window in the interior and the south is not walking time, air-conditioned transport stops being a luxury, and a twenty-five-minute walk suggested by a map at three in the afternoon in Seville in August is bad advice. Recognise the phrase 'ola de calor' — heatwave — and the AEMET colour alerts: yellow, orange, red. And note that this is precisely why the Spanish day is shaped the way it is: the long lunch and the late dinner are not laziness, they're physics.

exemplos.es: Un agua bien fría, por favor.
